Hyperalgesia and allodynia

Animal studies often report lower evoked hyperalgesia or allodynia after PBM. In a rat restraint-stress model, 808-nm treatment reduced visceral responses at some power settings but not at 3.5 mW or 1 W. No human study was identified.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Animal studies often report lower evoked hyperalgesia or allodynia after PBM. In a rat restraint-stress model, 808-nm treatment reduced visceral responses at some power settings but not at 3.5 mW or 1 W. No human study was identified.

Summary of the Evidence

After removing one red-light pain-model paper classified as non-PBM, the mapped hyperalgesia and allodynia categories contain 13 unique therapeutic animal publications: nine rat and four mouse reports. There are no human clinical studies or reviews in this set. The models range from inflammatory pain and nerve injury to visceral hypersensitivity, so they do not represent a single patient condition.

Human and clinical evidence

No direct human PBM treatment study for hyperalgesia or allodynia was identified. Pain-related outcomes in other indications are not counted here as clinical evidence for this category.

Animal evidence

Most studies report reduced evoked pain sensitivity in rodents after PBM, including models of nerve injury, inflammatory pain and allodynia. Findings vary by dose, timing and model. Ishibashi et al. tested 808-nm PBM in rats with restraint-stress-induced visceral hyperalgesia. Abdominal responses were reduced at average powers of 18, 70 and 460 mW, but not at 3.5 mW or 1 W, indicating that effects were not simply larger at the highest tested power (Ishibashi et al. 2024). A mouse CRPS-like model found reduced mechanical and thermal hypersensitivity after 660- or 830-nm light, with stronger effects reported at 660 nm (Rodrigues et al. 2020). Other papers measure inflammatory or sensory pathways alongside behavior, but those markers do not replace a pain outcome.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo study was identified. Cellular and tissue measurements are embedded in animal experiments.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Reported treatments include red visible light around 660 nm and near-infrared light around 808, 830 or 905 nm, delivered by laser or LED. Some studies vary power, wavelength or timing, while others use repeated local treatments after injury. The 808-nm dose-ranging study produced a non-linear pattern. Because the models, outcome tests and schedules differ, their results cannot define one clinical dose or predict relief in a particular chronic pain syndrome.

Interpretation

The publications support PBM-sensitive pain behavior in several rodent models, but they do not establish benefit for patients. Different experimental injuries and nonuniform dose responses are the main barriers to translating these findings into a clinical treatment estimate.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for pain relief in people because no human treatment study was identified. Low within animal models for reducing evoked hypersensitivity, with effects that vary by dose, timing and pain model.
Publications and records13 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Thirteen therapeutic animal publications report pain-threshold or hypersensitivity outcomes, but there are no patient trials and the models represent different injuries. One dose-ranging rat study found effects at some power settings but not at lower or higher settings. Human studies should use defined pain syndromes and report function and duration of relief.
